title: KV cache architecture & eviction troubleshooting - Elysium Labs (technical deep dive)
customer_attendees: Priya Nair - Head of ML Infra
summary: Deep technical session to troubleshoot KV cache evictions and paging behavior when serving long-context sessions. Covered eviction heuristics (LRU vs LFU), page-in delays, prefix reuse, batching interactions, quantization memory tradeoffs, and VPC/private deployment constraints. Agreed next steps: run targeted bench with Elysium's 100k long-context traces, share internal KV cache docs and eviction tuning guide, and schedule a 1:1 follow-up with infra team to test a configuration change on a staging Dedicated cluster.
transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2027-03-08 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 mins
Attendees: Samir (Redwood AE), Diana (Redwood SE), Marco (Redwood SE), Priya (Elysium Head ML Infra), Owen (Elysium Senior ML Eng), Jing (Elysium Platform Eng)
Links shared: internal benchmark sheet https://redwood.internal/benchmarks/kv-eviction-2027 (redwood link), security doc: https://redwood.docs/security-vpc.pdf

[00:00] Samir: hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. goal for today is to work through the eviction and paging issues you saw in staging with long-context sessions, and get to a concrete plan for a test on dedicated.
[00:28] Priya: yeah thanks. we're seeing pretty aggressive kv eviction after like 8k tokens in some sessions, and then the model latency spikes when the session resumes, which kills our SLOs. we don't want full on disk thrash.
[00:52] Diana: ok got it. quick clarifying q — when you say 8k tokens, is that per user session or aggregated across concurrent sessions?
[01:10] Owen: per session. it's mostly a conversation history where users paste long transcripts; a single session can go to 50k tokens but most active hotspot is 8-12k. we've tried increasing cache size but saw little improvement.
[01:32] Marco: thanks. two quick points up front: (1) our KV cache is sharded per GPU worker and uses a hybrid eviction policy (LRU + frequency decay) and (2) we do paging to local NVMe when memory exceeds threshold, but paging introduces a page-in latency penalty which you can observe as a spike.
[01:58] Jing: that aligns. in our logs we see "kv_cache_miss" bursts then the token latency goes from ~60ms to 450ms for a few seconds.
[02:18] Diana: perfect. would it be ok if we walk through the architecture and then look at your trace samples? want to surface where policy/config interplay might be causing the behavior.
[02:33] Priya: yep let's do trace first. i'll drop the 3 traces in the sheet.
[02:40] (file drop noted)

--- Trace review / architecture discussion ---
[03:05] Owen: first trace is user A long paste, then several prompt expansions; second is streaming interactive chat; third is multi-turn with repeated prefixes (the same system instructions repeated per turn).
[03:25] Diana: ok looking at trace 1 — i can already see that the prefix embeddings are unique per turn so prefix reuse is low, which increases KV key count. that's the main pressure.
[03:42] Marco: to expand, the KV store stores per-token keys (layer, position, head kv), so repeated system prompts that are identical can be reused via prefix dedupe; however your pipeline appears to regenerate slightly different tokens (whitespace/newline differences) so the hash differs and we can't dedupe.
[04:05] Priya: oh that's interesting — our frontend normalizes text but maybe not exactly. we'll audit whitespace.
[04:18] Samir: small differences can cause a different tokenization too. we sometimes normalize "strip trailing newline" to reduce unique prefixes.
[04:32] Owen: what about eviction policy — we changed to a pure LRU in staging because we thought recency mattered, but maybe frequency LFU with aging would help?
[04:46] Diana: yes LFU+decay helps for repeated prefixes across many sessions; hybrid gives recency for hot sessions and frequency for long-term repeats. but tuning the decay window is critical. your sessions that go 50k tokens will inevitably evict older keys unless you increase memory or use prefix dedupe.
[05:10] Jing: how about paging behavior? we saw lots of NVMe IO saturation when memory is hit. is there a recommended threshold for spilling?
[05:22] Marco: we recommend keeping spill threshold at ~85% of GPU host memory dedicated to the KV cache to avoid heavy tail paging. when we see heavy spill, page-in latency is high because random access patterns are common (not purely sequential).
[05:36] Diana: also worth noting that paging to local NVMe is faster than networked disk but still several ms per page. if your latency SLOs are tight, spilling is a non-starter.
[05:49] Priya: we have local NVMe on dedicated nodes; may need to tune. do you support background async prefetching?
[06:02] Marco: we do an async prefetcher for predicted next-segment keys when we see sequential usage, but it's heuristic-driven. for conversational workloads with lots of branching it's harder to prefetch accurately.
[06:18] Owen: would combining a disk-backed LRU plus a compact on-GPU bloom filter to quickly check membership help reduce noisy lookups?
[06:30] Diana: yes we actually maintain a compact in-memory index per worker — a 64-bit fingerprint table — but false positives can still cause page-in; tuning the fingerprint size helps. we can increase fingerprint bits to lower false positives at the cost of RAM.

--- Quantization and memory tradeoffs ---
[07:00] Samir: quick aside on quant: you're running 8-bit quant on your model, right?
[07:07] Priya: correct, mostly 8-bit int with some fp16 paths.
[07:12] Marco: quant affects KV size — lower precision reduces the size of cached values (the v in kv) but some kernels store intermediate mats in fp16 for perf; measured memory for KV per token reduced ~35% going from fp16 to 8-bit in our tests.
[07:30] Owen: did you see any stability/accuracy regressions with 8-bit and large context?
[07:36] Diana: minimal for our open models, but quantization noise can change similarity of cached vectors causing slightly different match rates for prefix reuse — in practice we saw 1-2% change. probably not the root of your eviction spike but worth noting.

--- Batching interactions ---
[08:10] Priya: we also noticed certain batch sizes cause more cache churn because the runtime groups diverse sessions and keys get interleaved. any suggestions?
[08:20] Marco: continuous batching is great for throughput, but heterogeneous requests that touch different contexts will increase working set. two levers: (1) batch segregation by session-heat (hot sessions grouped) and (2) adjustable batch window — shorter windows reduce interleaving at the expense of throughput.
[08:39] Samir: We can add a routing hint to keep long-context sessions on pinned workers so their KV stays warm. that's what Dedicated can enable (pinning + larger per-worker memory).
[08:52] Jing: yeah we were hoping Dedicated nodes would allow pinning. networking concerns: if we pin, does that impact failover behavior for redundancy?
[09:02] Diana: pinning reduces cross-worker redundancy. we recommend a small replication factor (2) for critical sessions; if a worker fails, the session falls back to a cold start on a replica. that tradeoff is usually acceptable vs full stateless scaling.

--- Paging/prefetch debug steps ---
[09:30] Marco: i'd like to walk through your metrics. can you show the timeline around one eviction event?
[09:37] (screen share / log snippet)
[09:45] Jing: here's a snippet: 15:12:03 kv_cache_miss spike -> 15:12:04 nvme_read_iops +60% -> 15:12:05 token_latency spike 420ms -> 15:12:10 recovery.
[10:05] Diana: ok you can see the page-in window is ~200-800ms depending on page size. two immediate tuning knobs: reduce page size (smaller pages reduce single read latency but increase metadata overhead) and increase NVMe queue depth.
[10:20] Priya: is there a recommended page size? we default to 1MB.
[10:27] Marco: 256KB-512KB often gives a better balance for random access workloads on good NVMe. 1MB tends to be better for sequential scans.
[10:40] Owen: how about pre-warming the cache at session start by streaming key prefixes?
[10:46] Diana: yes — if you have deterministically repeated prefixes we can prewarm at session init. the trick is not to prewarm too much or you'll thrash. we can prewarm top-N prefixes heuristically based on historical freq.

--- Prefix reuse and tokenization ---
[11:20] Marco: earlier Diana mentioned tokenization differences. easiest quick-win: normalize whitespace/newline and canonicalize system messages to exact bytes so tokenization yields identical sequences. canonical system message + message hashing => much better reuse.
[11:40] Priya: that seems low effort. we'll add canonicalization to the ingestion pipeline.
[11:48] Owen: do you support prefix dedupe across sessions globally or only per worker?
[11:55] Diana: dedupe is global at the control plane index but the actual KV storage is sharded; we maintain a global namespace for canonical prefixes and route duplicates to the same worker when possible. that routing is best-effort and can be tuned in Dedicated.
[12:15] Samir: note that global dedupe adds an extra lookup but saves downstream storage; there's a tradeoff in lookup overhead vs bandwidth.

--- Long-context and checkpointing ---
[12:38] Marco: for 50k token sessions we recommend logical checkpointing: summarize or compress earlier parts of the context into a smaller sketch representation stored in the KV as a compact vector so you don't need every token key. two approaches: (1) chunk-and-embed summaries, (2) learned compression with a lightweight model.
[12:59] Priya: we were already thinking to summarize earlier history. what's the recommended cadence? every 8-12k tokens?
[13:09] Diana: depends on conversation semantics; 8k is a reasonable start. you can test summarization loss vs memory saved with our optimize toolkit.

--- Network/VPC/on-prem specifics ---
[13:30] Jing: question on network: if we deploy Private in our VPC, does the KV cache ever cross network boundaries? we have strict egress rules.
[13:42] Marco: in Private mode the KV cache is local to the node pool you manage. traffic only crosses network boundaries during control-plane metadata sync which is minimal and can be constrained to your subnets. we can sign an appendix for no-cross-region sync.
[13:59] Samir: for Dedicated we can also pre-provision nodes in your VPC and disable any external DNS to meet compliance.

--- Deeper troubleshooting / root cause hypotheses ---
[14:20] Diana: synthesizing what's seen: root cause seems to be a combination of (1) high unique prefix cardinality due to slight token differences, (2) batch interleaving increasing working set, and (3) spill threshold too low causing NVMe thrash. each alone might be tolerable but together they cause the latency spikes.
[14:40] Priya: actionable then: canonicalize prefixes, reduce batch interleaving for long sessions, and raise spill threshold / change page size.
[14:52] Owen: any risks to raising the spill threshold? if we never spill we might OOM the node.
[14:58] Marco: right — you should raise incrementally and also monitor host memory pressure. we can also increase per-worker mem by using larger instance types on Dedicated.

--- Quick demo of config changes (SE-led) ---
[15:20] Diana: demo time; i'm going to change three flags in the runtime: prefix_normalization=true, spill_threshold=0.9, page_size=262144. watch the simulated trace.
[15:35] (demo - simulated run)
[15:50] Diana: see the working set stabilizes, nvme iops drop, and token latency stays ~80-90ms. obviously simulated load is a simplification.
[16:05] Priya: that looks promising. can you share the config snippet?
[16:10] Diana: will share after call; i already pasted the run config in the sheet.

--- Discussion: metrics to collect for a real test ---
[16:25] Marco: for the staging run we recommend collecting: per-token latency p50/p95/p99, kv_cache_hit_rate (per-prefix and per-token), nvme_iops, host_memory_free, spill_count, batch_window_ms, and worker routing heatmap.
[16:40] Priya: we'll wire those. any recommended thresholds? p95 < 250ms is our target, p99 < 500ms ideally.
[16:50] Samir: agreed. also collect payload sizes and tokenization diffs — we have a small script to compute canonicalization delta.

--- Cost/throughput tradeoffs ---
[17:10] Owen: what about cost — if we bump GPU instance size and memory, how much more expensive?
[17:18] Samir: there's a tradeoff. larger Dedicated nodes increase monthly cost but reduce operational latency; we can model cost per 1M tokens with and without prewarm/pinning. i'll send a TCO spreadsheet.
[17:30] Jing: do you have any auto-tiering or lifecycle to push cold keys to cheaper storage automatically?
[17:36] Marco: not yet automatic but we have an API to export cold keys to object storage and reinstate them on demand. that's a manual lifecycle. we can help scaffold a policy.

--- Security / compliance note ---
[17:55] Priya: quick security note — when we move to Dedicated in our VPC we need KMS integration and audit logs of KV access. is that supported?
[18:05] Diana: yes, Private/Dedicated supports customer-managed KMS and we emit audit logs for cache reads/writes. we'll share the SOC2 appendix.

--- Recap & next steps ---
[18:28] Samir: recap — immediate items: (1) Elysium will canonicalize prefixes in ingestion (Jing/Owen), (2) Redwood SEs will provide config snippet and recommended spill/page settings (Diana/Marco), (3) run a staging benchmark with 100k long-context traces and collect the metrics (Priya), (4) Redwood to provide TCO/sizing guidance for Dedicated and a security appendix (Samir).
[18:52] Priya: sounds good. timeline — can we run the staging bench this week and meet next Tuesday to review?
[19:00] Samir: yes we'll aim to have config snippet and docs by EOD tomorrow; bench results by Fri; follow-up next Tue 15:00 UTC?
[19:12] Owen: works for us.
[19:18] Jing: quick q — about prefix canonicalization, any recommended library or function?
[19:24] Marco: we'll share a small canonicalize_text.py snippet and a tokenization diff script.
[19:30] Diana: i'll also add a note about increasing fingerprint table bits if you still see false positives after canonicalization.
[19:40] Priya: thanks. any other open items?
[19:46] Samir: none from our side. thanks everyone.

End transcript.

Elysium to canonicalize prefixes in ingestion and run tokenization diff script on sample traces
Elysium to run staging benchmark (100k long-context traces) and share metrics sheet
Redwood to provide TCO/sizing guidance for Dedicated and security appendix (KMS, audit logs)
Schedule follow-up meeting: 2027-03-15T15:00:00Z to review results
